key_terms.meaning: Byte written to the 8255 control register that sets port A/B/C directions and the group A/B modes.
8255 mode where STB and ACK or IBF and OBF lines move each byte only when the peripheral is ready.
Register loaded with N so the output divides the input clock by N, or by N in BCD counting.
Counter state reached when the programmed count runs out; it sets the output or reloads the counter.
8-bit code the 8259 places on the data bus so the CPU jumps to the correct service routine.
Interrupt request register latches requests, in-service register marks the one being served, interrupt mask register blocks selected lines.
DMA request from the controller and hold acknowledge from the CPU granting bus ownership.
DMA cycle that moves one byte then returns the bus to the CPU; block mode keeps it longer.
Serial signalling rate in bits per second; the 8251 clock and mode/command settings set it.
Start bit, data bits, optional parity and stop bits that let the receiver find byte boundaries on one wire.
Turning on one digit at a time at high speed so shared segment lines appear to show all digits.
Register-select chooses command or data, read/write sets direction, enable latches the byte on its falling edge.
Smallest voltage step = Vref / 2^n for an n-bit converter; also called one LSB.
Converter that tests bits from MSB to LSB against a DAC output and keeps the nearest code.
Transistor, Darlington or relay driver that supplies motor or relay current while the port pin supplies only control current.
Ordered energising pattern of stator phases that moves the rotor one fixed step per pattern.
Fraction of period the output stays high; average voltage = D × Vhigh for duty D.
Timer compare match sets or clears a pin each period, giving a square wave whose high time is programmed.
Chip with battery-backed counters for seconds, minutes, hours and date, often with alarms, read over a serial or parallel bus.
Sensor output may be analog voltage, pulse train or serial digital word, so the CPU needs ADC, counter or UART respectively.

takeaways: The 8255 packs three ports into one control-word-programmed chip, so slow devices use handshake instead of forcing bus waits.
The 8253/8254 counts a known clock down to zero, producing delays, rates and waveforms without CPU loops.
The 8259 latches, masks and prioritises requests, then gives one vector so many devices share INTR.
The DMA controller moves bytes by taking HRQ/HLDA bus ownership, leaving the CPU out of the copy loop.
The 8251 frames each byte with start, parity and stop bits and converts between parallel and serial data.
Keyboards and displays use scanning and multiplexing because human-speed devices are slow but numerous.
ADC and DAC step size is set by reference voltage and bit count; code and voltage map linearly.
Motor and relay loads need external driver current; the CPU supplies only the step sequence or PWM duty.
Sensors and RTCs deliver analog, pulse or serial numbers; timers turn counts into PWM average voltage.

glossary.def: Programmable peripheral interface with three 8-bit ports whose directions and handshake modes are set by a control word.
Byte written to a programmable peripheral that selects its operating mode and data direction.
8255 simple input or output mode with no handshake lines.
8255 strobed input or output mode that uses port C lines for handshake and status.
8255 bit set/reset mode that sets or clears one selected bit of port C.
Programmable down-counter that divides its input clock and changes an output pin at terminal count.
8253/8254 control pin that enables, disables or restarts counting depending on the selected mode.
Counter value or state at which the programmed count ends and the output changes.
Programmable interrupt controller that latches, masks, prioritises and vectors eight interrupt request lines.
8259 register that blocks selected interrupt request lines from reaching the priority resolver.
Command sent to the 8259 after a service routine so the in-service bit is cleared.
Code supplied to the CPU that identifies the address of the interrupt service routine.
Chip that takes bus ownership and moves data between memory and a peripheral without the CPU copying each byte.
DMA method that takes the bus for one transfer at a time, briefly slowing the CPU.
Universal synchronous/asynchronous receiver-transmitter that converts parallel bytes to serial frames and back.
Number of serial signal bits per second, set by clock division and the USART mode.
Start, data, parity and stop bit structure that lets a serial receiver find byte boundaries.
Display of seven LED segments plus a decimal point, driven by a code for each digit.
Sharing wires by turning several devices or digits on one at a time faster than the eye can follow.
Liquid-crystal display driven by commands and data bytes through control lines such as RS, RW and E.
Analog-to-digital converter that maps an input voltage to the nearest binary code.
Digital-to-analog converter that maps a binary code to an output voltage.
Smallest voltage change a converter can represent, equal to Vref / 2^n for n bits.
Difference between the true analog value and the nearest code, at most half an LSB in ideal rounding.
Circuit that supplies the current or voltage needed by a motor, relay or lamp under a logic pin command.
Pulse-width modulation; a square wave whose duty cycle sets the average voltage delivered to a load.
